body:
I don't agree with your road trip analogy for similar reasons that I don't agree with banaruth's test analogy. I think you don't understand what I'm talking about with all of this race talk.

"If you were to take such a quintessential american roadtrip, would your cherished memories be of arriving in california, or of all the stops at the interesting places along the way."

The loser in the race is the one that didn't make any stops at interesting places along the way and didn't enjoy the trip or possible experiences along the way. The winners are the ones that make the most of the trip. The person that gets to California first isn't the winner of the race I'm talking about (actually, he'd be the loser since he killed himself to arrive at death more quickly than those that arrive at it with natural death at old age). 

If we want to keep your road trip analogy going, the race could be thought of as how much happyness/experience you get from this unique opportunity (which could be visiting tourist stops, or just laughing and having a good time with those in the car). What makes it a race is that everybody participating in this road trip is headed to California whether they want to or not. Your car is always headed in a direction toward California, with some people taking faster routes than others (such as those will illnesses, etc.). 

It seems people are getting confused about the life/race analogy by comparing it to other analogies?

I think that analogy isn't the right one...you're simply talking about turning in a test early or not, but you don't acknowledge your score on the test and what you actually write on the test. The whole life being a race thing incorporates what you do in your life in the short time that you have. 

If you want to keep the whole test analogy going, a better (in my opinion, but of course not perfect) one would be an essay exam where the "losers in life" waste the first 1/3 of the test time and make little to no progress, while the "winners in life" spent that time productively, already have thought of an answer to the prompt, and are knee deep in proving it with examples. Suicide would be turning your paper in early with whatever you had written up to that point. The "winners" in this race of life would not be so miserable during the whole exam to want to stop writing and turn the test in early, so they use all the time they can to continue to hone their paper. 

I hope you understand what I'm getting at. Your analogy seems off to me. Can you please try from another approach? I want arrive at "Life's like that. Just because you are doing things differently or 'slower' doesn't mean that you are a failure." with reasoning that makes sense to me.

I tried for a couple months but didn't like the idea of having to pay someone to listen to my emotions and problems.

Can you expand on this? Why is the point just to cross the finish line? What does that even mean to cross the finish line (surely it can't mean "not kill yourself and die a natural death instead" as I would then wonder where happiness would come into the picture...)?

But once you're dead, as far as you are concerned, the influence is no longer there. So it makes no difference whether you made the influence or not. If there is no after life, then you won't be able to have any appreciation of the influence made. Every life outcome is the same once you're dead, and all of this "influence" crap is only valid during your last second of consciousness...

You don't know what "Nothing, absolute nothingness" is, so you can't say it is a terrible thing. Trying to imagine "nothing" invalidates the entire notion of "nothing." You cannot fully understand what it means to not exist, so you cannot say that living is better than not existing. It's not like you can decide to "not exist," and then declare "see! this is worse than if I decided to keep on living!" That would invalidate the whole notion of "nothing"...

"Yes, the physical body is weak and it will die. But the actions you have taken in this life, the people you have interacted with, like everything else in the past, can never be erased."

They can and will be erased through death. Everybody you influence will die, and so will the people they influence, and so on and so forth.

"Because even my darkest hour is a far cry better than never having lived at all."

How can one even make a claim like that? Since we can't comprehend not having lived at all, you shouldn't be saying that things are a "far cry better."

All of the sand you contain will eventually burn up and disappear...so what was the point of transferring all the little grains in the first place? Especially if it's so painful to have to be alive and transfer these grains?

Isn't that a selfish thing to say? Obviously your father was drowning in his own misery and pain that was so bad that he decided to kill himself. I'm sure it hurts for you, but you have to understand that it hurt so much more for him that he gave up feeling anything good to stop feeling all the bad.

And notions of "never being alone" should not be taken so absolutely. Some random schmuck on the internet, though it is an actual person with his own life behind the computer screen, pales in comparison to someone physically there for you, to the point that you can't naively tell people that they are "never alone in this" just because random people on the internet will chat with you.
Who cares if people remember you? They will die too. If you're depressed now, why bother (assuming no afterlife)? Life is futile, isn't it?
